title: Verbalised Evaluation Awareness in Language Models Has Limited Effect on Behaviour
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: The study probes a model's behaviour under three interventions on evaluation-aware reasoning, each with a control, across several benchmarks.
layout: 3 stacked condition panels between input and output networks, left-to-right, control insets
description: A left-to-right experimental design diagram. On the left, a clipboard icon and a blue BENCHMARKS box list safety, alignment, moral decision making and political decision making. An arrow leads down to a neural-network icon labelled LRM. From the network, branching arrows fan out to three stacked orange rounded panels. The top panel, VEA Injection, shows a thought-cloud, a syringe and the sentence 'This is an evaluation.' A grey CONTROL inset shows a neutral sentence injected instead. The middle panel, VEA Removal, shows a scalpel and a struck-through cloud, with a grey CONTROL inset. The bottom panel, On-Policy Sampling, shows a die and two thought-clouds, one with 'This is an evaluation.' and one blank. The arrows merge into a second LRM on the right. An arrow leads up from it to a green BEHAVIOUR box listing harmfulness, misalignment, dilemma resolving and political opinions, next to a gavel icon. The orange panels in graded shades draw the eye first.
caption: Illustration of our three experimental conditions: injection and removal of VEA, each with a control, and on-policy sampling. Model outputs are evaluated across four benchmarks.
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) sometimes note in their chain of thought (CoT) that they may be under evaluation. Researchers worry that this verbalised evaluation awareness (VEA) causes models to adapt their outputs strategically, optimising for perceived evaluation criteria, which, for instance, can make models appear safer than they actually are. However, whether VEA actually has this effect is largely unknown. We tested this across open-weight LRMs and benchmarks covering safety, alignment, moral reasoning, and political opinion. We tested this both on-policy, sampling multiple CoTs per item and comparing those that spontaneously contained VEA against those that did not, and off-policy, using model prefilling to inject evaluation-aware sentences where missing and remove them where present, with subsequent resampling. VEA has limited effect on model behaviour: injecting VEA into CoTs produces near-zero effects ($Ï\leq 0.06$), removing it causes small shifts ($Ï\leq 0.12$) and spontaneously occurring VEA shifts answer distributions by at most 3.7 percentage points ($Ï\leq 0.31$). Our findings call for caution when interpreting high VEA rates as evidence of strategic behaviour or alignment tampering. Evaluation awareness may pose a smaller safety risk than the current literature assumes.
